problem: End-to-end RL/BC policies with embedding matching generalize poorly to unseen objects and environments and offer no action-level explanations, while zero-shot LLM+detector pipelines suffer error propagation, high inference cost, and cannot feed their reasoning back into the navigation policy.
motivation: Language-driven object navigation needs both fine-grained instance recognition (intrinsic and extrinsic attributes) and commonsense spatial reasoning. The authors argue agents should be Compact, Unified, Reasoning-capable and Explainable (CURE), and a small single VLA that reasons in image space over waypoint labels could meet all four.
key_idea: Fine-tune a 3B VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) with SFT on GPT-4o reasoning traces, then GSPO RL, to pick among waypoint labels overlaid on a panorama plus a top-down map, emitting <think>, <think_summary> and <action>.
insight: Explicit image-grounded reasoning makes the small VLA robust across splits: its OVON SR stays around 20-22 from Val Seen to Val Unseen, while RL baselines (DAgRL) fall from 41.30 to 18.30. RL post-training mainly improves efficiency (SPL) via better stopping, but only works with a Stop/non-Stop balanced RL set (otherwise reward hacking) and a nonzero KL term. Oracle Stop raises OVON Val Unseen SPL from 11.86 to 17.26 and CoIN Val Unseen SPL from 6.07 to 8.54, showing stop decisions and last-mile navigation are the bottleneck, together with Markovian (no-history) failures.
method: Waypoint candidate generation: three 90° RGB-D cameras form a 768×256 panorama; depth pixels are back-projected, obstacles and far points removed, DBSCAN clusters give centroids as candidate waypoints, which are drawn as randomly lettered red circles on the panorama.

Inputs: panoramic RGB, an online-built 256×256 top-down map (VLFM implementation), and the instruction; the output is a label choice or Stop, executed by Habitat's shortest-path planner (Forward 0.25m / Turn 15° / Stop). An extra Turn Around (180°) action is added at inference only.

Dataset (VISOR SFT set) from GOAT-Bench: unique-instruction episodes, ground-truth waypoint = candidate with minimum geodesic distance to the goal, GPT-4o CoT reasoning traces given GT info; 36,170 train / 3,047 val samples (1,698 stop in train).
SFT warm-up: teacher-forced cross-entropy on traces and structured tags, with random letter labels to avoid label memorization; one epoch on 2×H100 (~3.3 GPU-hours).

RL with GSPO: sequence-level importance ratio, group-normalized advantage, KL β=0.01 (β=0 hurts), 12 rollouts, frozen visual backbone; rewards are a small format reward (three tags) and an action reward (correct label or Stop). Stop is only in the text prompt and labels only in the image, forcing visual scanning.
Balanced RL dataset: episodes resampled to equal Stop and non-Stop ratio, since RL on the SFT data gave reward hacking (almost never Stop).
Oracle Stop analysis: overrides Stop when the true distance is under 1m, to isolate stopping errors.

setting.training_data: SFT set derived from GOAT-Bench: 36,170 train samples with GPT-4o reasoning traces; RL on a Stop-balanced subset of it. Trained on instance descriptions, not OVON categories.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (3×90° cameras, 768×256) + top-down map (256×256) + instruction; depth used only to build candidates and the map
setting.action_space: high-level waypoint label selection (plus Stop, Turn Around) executed by a shortest-path planner into Forward 0.25m / Turn 15° primitives
setting.privileged: none at test time (Oracle Stop variant uses GT distance to the target)

results: VISOR (GSPO) with 3B parameters reaches OVON Val Unseen SR 22.0 / SPL 11.86 and CoIN-Bench Val Unseen SR 9.37 / SPL 6.07, beating the RL baselines PSL (SPL 2.67) and Monolithic on CoIN Val Unseen and DAgRL on OVON Val Unseen (SR 18.30). It remains well below Uni-NaVid 7B (SR 39.5, SPL 19.80) and MTU3D (SR 40.8) on OVON Val Unseen, though Oracle Stop narrows the SPL gap to 17.26 vs 19.80.
limitations: Markovian setup with no history, causing last-mile failures and poor stop decisions (SR lags behind the strongest baselines).
Hallucinated labels, left-right spatial errors, and poor depth/distance estimation without explicit depth input.
Weak on seen splits versus specialized policies, and CoIN-Bench is small so results are noisy; RL sometimes stops prematurely.
